title: Why do interest rates matter so much?
seoTitle: Why Interest Rates Matter: Mortgages, Markets and Valuations Explained
seoDescription: Understand how interest rates affect borrowing, savings, mortgages, currencies, company valuations and financial markets.
excerpt: Interest rates are the price of money, influencing borrowing, saving, investment and asset valuations across the economy.
author: KitsuWire Editorial
keyTakeaways: Interest rates influence both the cost of borrowing and the return available on savings and bonds.
Higher rates can slow demand, investment and credit growth.
Rates affect asset valuations because future cash flows are discounted at different rates.
Markets react strongly to expectations about future rates, not only to the current policy rate.
body: Interest rates sit underneath much of the financial system. They determine how expensive it is to borrow money and how much return savers can earn for lending it.
Because rates influence households, companies, governments and investors at the same time, even small changes can ripple through mortgages, bond markets, currencies and stock valuations.

sections.heading: What an interest rate actually represents
paragraphs: An interest rate is the price paid for using money over time. Borrowers compensate lenders for delaying consumption, taking credit risk and accepting inflation risk.

Different rates exist across the economy. Central-bank policy rates influence short-term financial conditions, while mortgage, corporate and government bond rates reflect additional risks and market expectations.

sections.heading: How central banks influence rates
paragraphs: Central banks set or guide short-term policy rates to influence inflation and economic activity. Higher policy rates usually make financing more expensive; lower rates can encourage borrowing and spending.
The transmission is indirect. Banks, bond markets and borrowers react to both current policy and expectations about future inflation and growth.

sections.heading: Why mortgages and consumer credit react
paragraphs: When market rates rise, new mortgages and loans often become more expensive. Households then face higher monthly payments or reduce borrowing.
That can cool housing demand, durable-goods purchases and other interest-sensitive spending. The impact depends on whether borrowers use fixed or variable rates and how quickly loans reset.

sections.heading: Why rates affect company valuations
paragraphs: A company's value depends partly on the present value of future cash flows. When discount rates rise, those future cash flows are worth less in today's terms.
This effect can be especially important for companies whose expected profits lie far in the future. Higher borrowing costs can also directly reduce profits for highly leveraged businesses.

sections.heading: Bonds and the yield relationship
paragraphs: Existing bond prices generally move inversely to market yields. If new bonds offer higher yields, older lower-yielding bonds become less attractive unless their prices fall.
Longer-duration bonds are typically more sensitive to rate changes because more of their value depends on payments far in the future.

sections.heading: Why markets care about expectations
paragraphs: Financial markets continuously price what they expect central banks to do next. A rate cut can therefore be disappointing if investors had already expected an even larger cut.
Economic data on inflation, employment and growth matter partly because they change those expectations. Markets often move before the central bank acts.

faq.question: Why do stocks sometimes fall when rates rise?
faq.answer: Higher rates can reduce valuations, raise financing costs and make safer fixed-income assets more competitive with equities.

faq.question: Do higher rates always strengthen a currency?
faq.answer: No. Relative rates matter, but currencies also respond to growth expectations, risk sentiment and confidence in policy.

faq.question: What is a real interest rate?
faq.answer: A real interest rate adjusts a nominal rate for inflation, giving a better sense of the inflation-adjusted return or borrowing cost.
